source_title: KFC UK 2018 chicken-supply / distribution crisis (named journalism: CNN, BBC reporting on the DHL distribution switch)
publisher_issuer: Named journalism (CNN; corroborated by BBC and contemporaneous UK reporting)
company_context: KFC's UK operation (largely run through franchisees, ~80% of outlets) switched its logistics/distribution contract from Bidvest Logistics to DHL in February 2018. The new arrangement, run from a single warehouse, failed almost immediately, leaving most UK KFC restaurants without chicken.
macro_context: A cost-driven supplier/logistics change with no transition overlap; the prior distributor (Bidvest) operated six warehouses while the new provider (DHL) relied on a single Rugby depot, removing redundancy from a fresh-food supply chain.
evidence_summary: After DHL took over deliveries from Bidvest Logistics on 14 February 2018, the supply chain collapsed within roughly 48 hours. More than two-thirds of KFC's UK outlets closed; by 18 February only 266 of about 870 restaurants in the UK and Ireland remained open. The single-warehouse model lacked the capacity, staffing and redundancy of the previous six-warehouse arrangement, causing mishandling and spoilage. KFC issued a widely praised apology ('FCK') advertisement, and within a few weeks about 97% of restaurants had reopened. KFC subsequently dropped DHL and returned distribution control to Bidvest. Reported same-store sales growth was around -6.8% in the affected period.
owner_decision_context: KFC chose DHL primarily for lower cost and cut over from Bidvest overnight with no transition overlap, concentrating fresh-food distribution in a single warehouse and removing the redundancy that had previously absorbed disruptions.
action_taken: KFC issued a public apology campaign, prioritised reopening, and within weeks reversed the decision by dropping DHL and returning distribution to Bidvest; franchisees (covering ~80% of outlets) were supported and offered compensation arrangements.
outcome_evidence: Rapid reopening (~97% within weeks) and the reversion to Bidvest confirm a recoverable temporary operational shock rather than a solvency event; the brand and network survived intact despite a sharp short-term sales hit (~-6.8% same-store).
source_limitations: WebFetch typically 403s here; figures confirmed verbatim in WebSearch snippets attributed to CNN and contemporaneous reporting. The '266 of ~870' and '97% reopened' figures are widely reported; the '-6.8% same-store' and turnover figures appear in secondary supply-chain case writeups rather than a single primary filing, so the -6.8% is treated as reported, not primary-verified.
directly_stated: DHL took over from Bidvest on 14 February 2018
More than two-thirds of UK outlets closed; only 266 of ~870 open by 18 February 2018
Bidvest used 6 warehouses vs DHL's single Rugby depot
~97% of restaurants reopened within a few weeks; KFC reverted to Bidvest
inferred: Optimising distribution purely on cost while removing redundancy created a single-point-of-failure operational bottleneck
The event was a transient shock, recoverable because the underlying demand and brand were intact
why_useful_for_opsiq: Clean example of a temporary operational-bottleneck shock with full recovery, distinct from financial-distress cases. Tests whether the engine classifies a single-point-of-failure supply-chain disruption as a recoverable operational shock (outcome 13), recommends restoring redundancy, and avoids mislabelling a transient event as terminal failure.
